nameStory: This moth gets its name from a clever magic trick it performs when threatened. While resting, it shows only drab brown forewings that blend perfectly with tree bark, but when startled, it suddenly flashes brilliant yellow-orange hindwings – like revealing a bright yellow petticoat underneath a plain brown dress!
description: The Large Yellow Underwing is a hefty night-flying moth that's become one of New England's most common species since arriving from Europe in the 1980s. With a wingspan of 2-2.4 inches, it's quite substantial – about the size of a small bat when flying. The forewings range from light brown to nearly black and often look mottled or streaky, while the hidden hindwings are a stunning bright orange-yellow with black borders. This is one of the cutworm moths, meaning its caterpillars are notorious garden pests that chew through plant stems at ground level.

idTips.label: Hidden bright underwings
idTips.description: When the moth opens its wings or takes flight, brilliant orange-yellow hindwings with black borders flash into view – a stark contrast to the drab brown forewings

idTips.label: Variable brown forewings
idTips.description: Upper wings range from light brown to almost black with mottled patterns; darker individuals often show a pale streak along the leading edge that feels smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Substantial size and weight
idTips.description: This is a notably heavy, robust moth with a 2-2.4 inch wingspan – you can feel its weight if it lands on your hand, unlike smaller, more delicate moths

idTips.label: Strong attraction to lights
idTips.description: Masses around porch lights, street lamps, and lit windows at night, sometimes arriving in overwhelming numbers that can carpet the ground beneath lights

idTips.label: Night-flying behavior
idTips.description: Active from dusk through dawn during summer months, with a heavy, somewhat erratic flight pattern quite different from the fluttery movement of smaller moths

habitat: Large Yellow Underwings are found throughout New England in virtually any habitat where plants grow – gardens, fields, forest edges, suburban yards, and even urban areas. They're particularly common around human settlements where outdoor lighting attracts them in large numbers. The caterpillars live in soil and leaf litter around the base of herbaceous plants, making them ubiquitous wherever there's vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; overwintering pupae are developing underground in soil and garden beds.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season from July through August when adults are most commonly seen swarming around lights at night. This is when mating and egg-laying occurs.
seasonality.fall: Flight continues into September, with numbers gradually declining. Late-season individuals may appear more worn and faded than fresh summer moths.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity; the species overwinters as pupae buried in soil, waiting for warm weather to emerge as adults.

funFact: This European invader has conquered North America faster than almost any other moth – spreading from Nova Scotia to Alaska in just 20 years, making it one of the most successful insect invasions in modern history!
confusionNotes: The bright yellow underwings make this species unmistakable when wings are spread, but resting individuals with closed wings can be confused with other brown moths. Remember: if it's brown, heavy-bodied, and attracted to lights in summer, try gently disturbing it to see if yellow underwings flash – that's your definitive ID trick.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Large' Yellow Underwing, this refers to size relative to other yellow underwing species in Europe, not necessarily other moths in New England. The 'cutworm' name comes from the caterpillars' habit of cutting plant stems at soil level, often killing entire seedlings overnight – making gardeners both familiar with and frustrated by this species.
compareHints: This is the only yellow underwing species established in New England, making identification easier than in its native Europe where multiple similar species occur. Among New England's cutworm moths, it's distinguished by its large size, bright yellow (not orange or red) underwings, and extremely variable brown forewings that can range from tan to nearly black.
